subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

repairs.why:
FIRST-VISIT ORDER, wave 2 of S5's corpus (2026-08-12). p11's U5 'Observe and Classify Paper Types' is the first visit to 'Different Types of Paper and their Uses' — the registry's LAST section — arriving before sections 2, 3 and 4 are taught at all. Coverage is tracked as a single frontier, so any truncated serve of p11 (X=9, X=10) would have taught section 5 while the frontier claimed the whole registry was covered, under-reporting the drop. The move puts U5 immediately before U11, its own section's other unit. Founder ruling 2026-08-12, declared a ONE-OFF on this compact alone.
THE TOP IS NOT AT FAULT AND IS NOT TOUCHED: the chapter summary's section order — taken from the textbook — is exactly the registry order (How Paper is Made / Making Responsible Choices / Let Us Get Creative / Let us reflect / Different Types), so the top is faithful to the source and p11 is the deviant. p08, the other compact, already keeps the section last and passes.
SAFE: the two units are the same section and read as a pair once adjacent — U5 observes and matches samples to the Textbook p. 123 table, U11 'completes any remaining portions' of that same table, so U11's existing backward dependency gets stronger, not weaker. Neither names content from sections 2-4, and each item follows its own unit through the remap.

repairs.reason: register backfill (founder ruling 2026-08-02; testing.md C3 / ARV-D-011..013, ARV-D-026)

edits.note: 'what exactly will you do differently?' is the prompt that makes a vague step specific; the morning is a calendar Aruvi does not model

periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Students discuss whether we waste paper and how we might reduce that wastage (p. 122)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figures showing Pihu's story and paper-making steps

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up several everyday paper objects (textbook, newspaper, a napkin) and asks: What do all of these have in common? Students share ideas freely. Teacher notes responses on the board, guiding the class toward the idea that all paper comes from trees.

Students open Textbook p. 122 and read the discussion prompts together. Teacher leads a whole-class conversation: Do we waste paper? How do you know? Students share examples from home and school — tearing out only a few lines from a full page, using paper once and throwing it away. Teacher connects these examples to the fact that paper production requires large numbers of trees, water, and energy.

Teacher introduces the historical writing materials used in India — cloth, leaves, wooden boards, and palm leaves (talapatra) — drawing these out through questions: What did people write on before paper existed? Why might those materials have been chosen? Students discuss how the natural environment shaped these choices.
Class shares two or three concrete ideas for reducing paper waste in their own classroom. Teacher records these on the board. Students copy the ideas into their notebooks as a personal reference.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect everyday material use to the natural resources required to produce that material.
periods.section_context: Paper made from trees, drawing books, newspapers, paper napkins, chart papers; historical writing materials — cloth, leaves, wooden boards, palm leaves (talapatra); paper production requiring trees, water, and energy.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether their grandparents or elders have mentioned any materials other than paper used for writing or wrapping — this draws out local memory of traditional practices naturally in conversation.

periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Make recycled paper using old newspapers, fenugreek seeds, and water through soaking, pulping, rolling, and drying (p. 119)
materials: Old newspapers (torn into small pieces, pre-soaked overnight in water brought by teacher)
Water in a basin or bucket
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 119 step-by-step illustration of the paper-making process

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the idea that paper comes from wood pulp and introduces today's activity: making recycled paper. Students open Textbook p. 119 and read through the steps before touching any materials.

In small groups, students mash or blend the pre-soaked newspaper and fenugreek seed mixture into a smooth pulp. Teacher circulates, encouraging students to describe the texture: How does the pulp feel? What has happened to the newspaper? Why do you think fenugreek seeds are added?

Each group spreads their pulp onto a flat tray or plastic sheet and uses a rolling pin to flatten it into a thin, even sheet, following the guidance on Textbook p. 119. Teacher checks that sheets are not too thick and guides groups to even out lumpy patches.

Sheets are set aside to begin drying (they will continue to dry undisturbed). Students record in their notebooks: the materials used, the steps followed, and what they observed about the pulp at each stage. Teacher asks: What do you think will happen to the sheet as it dries?

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a multi-step making process by following sequential instructions and recording observations at each stage.
periods.section_context: Old newspapers, fenugreek seeds (methi), water; pulp-making steps — soaking, mashing, spreading, rolling, drying; recycled paper sheet.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Pose the open question: Why might fenugreek seeds work as a binding material? — allow students to hypothesise before moving on, rather than explaining the answer immediately.

periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Colour pieces of recycled paper using natural ingredients from the table, keeping quantity equal, and record observations (p. 120)
materials: Pieces of plain paper cut to equal size (commercial or from previous session's dried sheets if available, otherwise commercial)
Natural colouring ingredients: turmeric, beetroot juice, spinach leaf, marigold petals, henna powder (or any locally available plant-based colour sources)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 120 table of natural ingredients and observation format

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens a brief discussion: Where do the colours on cloth, pots, and paper come from? Students guess. Teacher introduces natural dyes — colours made from plant parts (leaf, flower, root, seed, stem) — as traditional, safe colouring agents, drawing on Textbook p. 120.

In pairs or small groups, students apply a different natural ingredient to each equal-sized paper piece, keeping the quantity of ingredient the same for each. They observe and compare the colour produced and whether it soaks in or sits on the surface. Students refer to Textbook p. 120 for the ingredient table and observation format.

Students record their observations in a table in their notebooks: ingredient name, colour produced, how bright or faint it is. Teacher prompts: Which ingredient gave the strongest colour? Which barely showed? What might explain the difference?
Whole-class share-out: groups report their strongest and weakest colours. Teacher notes results on the board. Students add a brief conclusion line to their notebook table.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a controlled comparison by keeping one variable constant and recording how different inputs produce different observable outcomes.
periods.section_context: Natural dyes from plant parts — leaf, flower, root, seed, stem; turmeric, beetroot, spinach, marigold, henna; equal-sized paper pieces; observation table of colour and brightness.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether anyone at home uses natural ingredients to colour food, cloth, or skin for festivals — this surfaces local knowledge of plant-based dyes without labelling it as a separate topic.

periods.activity_title: Greeting Card or Paper Mask from Recycled Paper
periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Make a greeting card, paper mask, or similar item from recycled paper (p. 121)
materials: Recycled paper pieces (commercial paper acceptable if session 2 sheets are not ready)
Natural colour materials from previous experiment or crayons
Scraps of old newspaper for additional texture
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 121 examples of items made from recycled paper

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows Textbook p. 121 and invites students to choose what they will make — a greeting card, a paper mask, or another item of their own design using recycled paper. Students decide and gather the materials they need.

Students create their chosen item, cutting, folding, gluing, and decorating. Teacher circulates and asks each student to explain their design choices: Why did you choose this shape? What will this card be used for? Encouragement is given to use natural colours from the earlier experiment where possible.
Students write a one- or two-sentence caption on the back of their item or in their notebook explaining what it is made from and why they chose recycled paper to make it.

A quick gallery walk: students place their items on their desks and walk around to look at others' work. Teacher closes with: What does it feel like to make something useful from something that would have been thrown away?

periods.implied_lo: Students can use locally available materials to create a functional or decorative object and explain the material choices behind it.
periods.section_context: Recycled paper, old newspaper scraps, natural colours; greeting card, paper mask, student-chosen paper item.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students who finish early to add a written message to their card or further decorate their mask — keep the focus on the quality of making rather than speed of completion.

periods.textbook_anchor: Making Responsible Choices — Discuss situations with classmates and write which of the 5Rs each belongs to (p. 125)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 125 table of situations (Maya, Rohan, Sara, Kabir, Priya, shopkeeper)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the 5Rs — Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle — writing each on the board with one concrete example. Students read the definitions from Textbook p. 125 and discuss in pairs: Which R feels easiest to do at home?

Students open Textbook p. 125 and work through the table of situations in small groups: Maya and the plastic straw, Rohan and old notebook pages, Sara giving books to younger students, Kabir painting an old bottle, Priya making a bag from old clothes, the shopkeeper folding newspapers into envelopes. Each group decides which R each situation belongs to and writes it down with a short reason.

Groups share their answers. Where groups disagree, teacher facilitates a short debate: could this situation belong to more than one R? Teacher draws out that some situations sit at the boundary between, say, Reuse and Repurpose, and that reasoning matters more than the single right label.
Each student adds one situation from their own life to their notebook and labels it with the correct R. Teacher invites two or three volunteers to share.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify everyday actions into a conservation framework and justify the classification with a reason.
periods.section_context: 5Rs — Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle; situations involving Maya (plastic straw), Rohan (notebook pages), Sara (books), Kabir (bottle), Priya (bag), shopkeeper (newspaper envelopes); Braille as specialised paper use.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether they have seen shopkeepers or family members make packets from newspaper or old paper — this surfaces local Repurpose practices that may not appear in the textbook examples.

periods.activity_title: Paper Waste and the 5Rs — Connecting to Our World
periods.textbook_anchor: Making Responsible Choices — Discuss situations with classmates and write which of the 5Rs each belongs to (p. 125)

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the 5Rs by asking: Without looking at your notes, can you recall all five Rs? Students reconstruct the framework from memory. Teacher confirms and writes the five Rs on the board.

Class discussion: How does reducing paper waste help trees, water, and energy? Students connect the 5Rs to the resource costs of paper-making discussed in the opening unit of the chapter. Teacher probes: If every student in this school used both sides of every sheet, how might that change things? Students reason aloud.

Students write a personal 5Rs pledge in their notebook — one concrete action for each R that they can realistically take in their own school or home life. Teacher circulates and encourages specific, doable actions rather than vague statements.
Students share their Reduce and Refuse pledges with a partner and give each other one piece of feedback: Is this action specific enough to actually do? Partners refine their pledges if needed.

periods.implied_lo: Students can propose specific personal conservation actions linked to a named environmental principle and evaluate whether those actions are realistic and precise.
periods.section_context: 5Rs pledge — Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle; connection between paper reduction and conservation of trees, water, energy.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students to think about which R is hardest to practise in their family's daily life and why — this moves the conversation from ideal behaviour to the real constraints people face.

periods.activity_title: Transforming Paper into Toys and Decorations
periods.section_ref: Let Us Get Creative with Paper
periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Make a greeting card, a paper mask or any such item made of recycled paper (p. 121)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figures showing newspaper figures, paper fans, and decorative birds

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays or describes examples of paper toys and decorations — a newspaper figure, a folded fan, a paper bird. Students discuss: What do all these have in common? Where do the raw materials come from? Teacher connects this directly to the Repurpose principle.

Students choose one item to make — a paper fan, a folded or twisted newspaper figure, or a decorative bird — using only old or used paper and basic craft supplies. Teacher encourages students to think before cutting: plan your shape, then make it. Students work individually or in pairs.
Students write a label for their item stating: what it is, what paper it was made from, and which R of the 5Rs it demonstrates. The label is attached to or placed beside the item.

Brief share: students hold up their item and read their label aloud. Teacher highlights the variety of forms created from the same waste material and asks: Does making something new from old paper feel different from throwing it away?

periods.implied_lo: Students can transform a discarded everyday material into a new object and articulate the environmental principle that this action represents.
periods.section_context: Old newspaper, used paper; newspaper figures, paper fans, decorative birds; Repurpose as one of the 5Rs.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether family members or community artisans make useful objects from paper or other discarded materials at home — draw out local craft traditions that embody repurposing.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting on Paper Pulp Objects and the 5Rs in My Life
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Write down one step you can take for each of the 5Rs in the boxes given below (p. 127)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 127 reflection boxes and table

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 127. Teacher reads the first reflection prompt aloud: What objects can be made from paper pulp? Students brainstorm individually for a short time, then share with the class. Teacher adds ideas from elders and craftspeople that students may not have considered — papier-mâché bowls, seedling pots, paper clay toys.

Students complete the second reflection task from Textbook p. 127: writing one specific step they can take for each of the five Rs in the boxes provided. Teacher circulates and prompts students whose steps are vague: instead of 'use less paper', what exactly will you do differently?

Students work on the third reflection task from Textbook p. 127: completing the table of changes they can bring in daily life using the 5Rs to avoid paper wastage. Teacher encourages students to think across different settings — home, classroom, market, festivals.
Students read one entry from their table to a partner. Partners check: Is this a real change or just a wish? Students revise any entries that are too vague.

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply a multi-principle conservation framework to their own daily context and generate specific, actionable commitments for each principle.
periods.section_context: Paper pulp objects — papier-mâché bowls, seedling pots, paper clay toys; personal 5Rs steps; daily life changes table.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students to think about a family celebration or festival where a lot of paper is used and wasted — what could be changed for that occasion? This grounds the reflection in a concrete, culturally familiar context.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Discuss the changes you can bring in your daily life by using 5Rs rule to avoid wastage of paper (p. 127)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with Textbook p. 127's discussion prompt: What changes can we bring in our daily life using the 5Rs to avoid wasting paper? Students share entries from their reflection table (completed in the previous work on this section). Teacher records key ideas on the board in a class-wide table under the five Rs.

Class debates: Which of the five Rs is easiest to practise at school? Which is hardest? Students give reasons based on their own experience. Teacher probes: Does it depend on what resources your family has? Does it depend on what is available in your area? This surfaces the real-life constraints behind conservation choices.

Students write a short paragraph in their notebooks: two or three changes they have genuinely decided to make, and the reason behind each choice. Teacher emphasises that the strength of the writing lies in the reason, not just the action.
Two or three students read their paragraphs aloud. Class offers one appreciative observation per reader: What made that commitment specific and believable?

periods.implied_lo: Students can evaluate conservation choices in the context of real constraints and construct a reasoned personal commitment to specific behaviour changes.
periods.section_context: 5Rs in daily life — school and home settings; reasons behind conservation choices; constraints on conservation practice; personal written commitment.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: If someone in your family says they cannot afford to refuse the free paper bag at the market, what could they do instead? — this opens a discussion about Reduce and Reuse as practical alternatives when Refuse is not possible.

periods.section_ref: Different Types of Paper and their Uses
periods.textbook_anchor: Different Types of Paper and their Uses — Observe different types of paper, paste small pieces, and write their uses (p. 123)
materials: Small pieces of writing paper, newspaper, art paper, cardboard, and tissue paper (one set per pair)
Notebook or loose sheet for pasting

time_bands.activity: Teacher places the five paper samples on each pair's desk. Students handle each one without yet naming them. Teacher asks: Without looking at the labels, can you sort these into groups? What are you noticing about how they feel, how they bend, how they tear?

Students open Textbook p. 123 and match their samples to the named types — writing paper, newspaper, art paper, cardboard, tissue paper. They paste a small piece of each type into their notebook in the format shown in the textbook and write one or two uses beside each.

Teacher leads a brief discussion: Why is tissue paper thin and soft? Why is cardboard thick and hard? Students connect the property of the paper to its purpose. Teacher notes key properties on the board: thickness, softness, absorbency, stiffness.
Students write a short summary sentence in their notebook: two paper types, their key property, and their most important use. Teacher collects or checks notebooks briefly.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe the physical properties of everyday materials, classify them by those properties, and connect each property to a specific human use.
periods.section_context: Writing paper, newspaper, art paper, cardboard, tissue paper; properties — thickness, softness, absorbency, stiffness; uses of each paper type.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students to name one paper type they use at home that is different from those on the table — this widens observation beyond the classroom sample set.

periods.activity_title: Paper All Around — Properties, Purposes, and Responsible Use
periods.section_ref: Different Types of Paper and their Uses
periods.textbook_anchor: Different Types of Paper and their Uses — Observe different types of paper that we use in daily life, paste small pieces, and write their uses (p. 123)
materials: Small samples of writing paper, newspaper, art paper, cardboard, tissue paper

time_bands.activity: Teacher hands out paper samples and asks students to feel each one carefully. Discussion: Which paper type uses the most material? Which uses the least? Which do you think takes the most trees to produce? Students reason from their observations about thickness and stiffness.

Students open Textbook p. 123 and complete any remaining portions of the classification table — pasting sample pieces and writing uses for any paper types not yet recorded. Teacher ensures every student has a complete table with all five paper types.

Students choose one paper type from the table and write three sentences: the property that makes it useful, the resource cost of making it, and one way they can use it more responsibly. They refer to what the chapter has covered about trees, water, and energy in paper production.

Whole-class closing discussion: If you had to choose one type of paper to use less of, which would it be and why? Students justify their choice using both material properties and resource costs. Teacher thanks the class for their thinking and encourages them to carry their observations beyond the classroom.

periods.implied_lo: Students can link the observed physical properties of a material to the natural resources required to produce it and propose a responsible use decision based on that connection.
periods.section_context: Writing paper, newspaper, art paper, cardboard, tissue paper; properties — thickness, softness, absorbency, stiffness; resource costs — trees, water, energy; responsible use choice.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether any paper type on the table could be replaced by something else — a cloth, a leaf, a board — and what that replacement would cost or save. This loops back to the chapter's opening discussion of historical writing materials.

assessment_items.question_text: Pihu learns that paper is made from trees. Which of the following is needed in large quantities to make paper from wood pulp?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. This item checks whether students recall the resource cost of industrial paper-making as introduced in the opening discussion of the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect everyday material use to the natural resources required to produce that material.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has not connected paper-making to trees and water; may be confusing with brick or pottery production.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student is blending the home recycled-paper activity (fenugreek seeds) with the industrial process — a within-chapter confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student is thinking of metal or industrial manufacturing unrelated to paper, suggesting the connection between trees and paper was not retained.

assessment_items.question_text: Write the steps you would follow to make recycled paper at home using old newspapers and fenugreek seeds. List the steps in the correct order.
expected_elements: Tear old newspaper into small pieces and soak them in water (with fenugreek seeds) for an adequate time.
Mash or blend the soaked mixture into a smooth pulp.
Spread the pulp onto a flat surface and roll it into a thin, even sheet.
Leave the sheet to dry completely.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per element. Full marks require all four steps in a logical sequence. Accept reasonable paraphrase of each step.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a multi-step making process by following sequential instructions and recording observations at each stage.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

expected_elements: Tear old newspaper into small pieces and soak them in water (with fenugreek seeds) for an adequate time.
Mash or blend the soaked mixture into a smooth pulp.
Spread the pulp onto a flat surface and roll it into a thin, even sheet.
Leave the sheet to dry completely.

assessment_items.question_text: In the natural colour experiment, Riya used turmeric on one piece of paper and spinach on another. She kept the size of the paper pieces the same and used the same quantity of each ingredient. Why was it important to keep the quantity the same? What did keeping it the same help her find out?
expected_elements: Keeping the quantity the same made the comparison fair — one variable (the ingredient) was changed while everything else stayed the same.
This allowed Riya to conclude that any difference in colour or brightness was due to the ingredient, not the amount used.
It helped her compare which natural ingredient produces a stronger or brighter colour on paper.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per element. The key understanding is that equal quantity makes the comparison valid. Accept any answer that conveys the idea of a fair test.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a controlled comparison by keeping one variable constant and recording how different inputs produce different observable outcomes.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Keeping the quantity the same made the comparison fair — one variable (the ingredient) was changed while everything else stayed the same.
This allowed Riya to conclude that any difference in colour or brightness was due to the ingredient, not the amount used.
It helped her compare which natural ingredient produces a stronger or brighter colour on paper.

assessment_items.task: Make a greeting card or paper mask using only old newspaper or used paper. On the back of your item (or in your notebook), write two sentences: (1) what your item is made from, and (2) why you chose recycled paper to make it.
assessment_items.scaffold: My item is a ___. I made it from ___. I chose recycled paper because ___.
format_of_output: A handmade greeting card or paper mask using old/used paper
Two written sentences on the back or in notebook
assessment_items.annotation: Assess both the object and the written caption. A strong response names the material (old newspaper / used paper) and gives a reason connected to recycling or reducing waste rather than a personal preference alone.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use locally available materials to create a functional or decorative object and explain the material choices behind it.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students show they can translate knowledge of recycling into a creative act and articulate the environmental reasoning behind their material choice.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students to name the material and give a reason. Look for whether the reason reflects chapter learning (saves trees, reduces waste) rather than a surface comment (it was available).
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: item is made from clearly recognisable waste paper; written reason explicitly connects the choice to saving trees, reducing waste, or the Repurpose principle. Weak: item uses fresh paper; reason is vague or absent.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find writing difficult may dictate their two sentences to the teacher or a peer. Students with mobility limitations may tear and paste rather than cut. The item can be as simple as a folded card.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The creative-and-explain format matches the C&E dominant mode and the competency's requirement to use local materials to create an object for display or use.

assessment_items.question_text: Ananya is choosing paper for different tasks. She needs a material that is thick, hard, and good for making boxes. Which type of paper should she choose?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This item tests whether students can match a named material property (thick, hard) to the correct paper type and use.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Different Types of Paper and their Uses
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe the physical properties of everyday materials, classify them by those properties, and connect each property to a specific human use.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has confused softness and thinness (tissue) with hardness — has not connected the property to the use.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may be thinking of a commonly available paper without connecting its properties (thin, flimsy) to the requirement for thickness and hardness.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be conflating art paper (smooth, used for drawing) with cardboard, perhaps because both are used for creative activities.

assessment_items.question_text:
Look at the situations below. Write which R of the 5Rs each situation belongs to, and give one reason for your answer.
(a) Kabir paints an old glass bottle and uses it as a flower vase.
(b) Maya refuses to use a plastic straw when she drinks juice.
expected_elements: (a) Repurpose — Kabir is giving the old bottle a completely new use (flower vase) rather than throwing it away.
(b) Refuse — Maya is choosing not to use the disposable item in the first place, stopping the waste before it starts.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per correctly labelled and justified pair. Accept Reuse for part (a) if the student gives a reasonable explanation (bottle still used), but prompt the distinction between Reuse and Repurpose if time allows.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify everyday actions into a conservation framework and justify the classification with a reason.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

(b) Refuse — Maya is choosing not to use the disposable item in the first place, stopping the waste before it starts.

assessment_items.task: Write your personal 5Rs pledge. For each of the five Rs — Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle — write one specific action you will take to reduce paper waste. Make sure each action is something you can actually do at school or at home.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Refuse: I will refuse ___.
Reduce: I will reduce ___.
Reuse: I will reuse ___.
Repurpose: I will repurpose ___.
Recycle: I will recycle ___.
format_of_output: Five written pledge statements, one per R
assessment_items.annotation: Assess specificity and feasibility. A strong response names a concrete object or situation for each R (e.g. 'I will refuse extra printouts the teacher does not need me to keep'). Vague entries like 'I will use less paper' without naming what or when are weak.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can propose specific personal conservation actions linked to a named environmental principle and evaluate whether those actions are realistic and precise.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students show they can internalise each of the five conservation principles and translate them into realistic, context-specific commitments in their own lives.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Each line should name a specific object, habit, or situation. Look for whether the student distinguishes between the Rs — a student who writes 'use less' for all five has not yet internalised the distinctions.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: each pledge names a specific material, situation, or occasion; the action is clearly doable by a Grade IV student. Weak: pledges are generic or identical across Rs; student cannot distinguish Reuse from Repurpose.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may write in their home language if needed and translate key words. Students who struggle with writing may draw their pledge action and label it.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Writing a personal pledge for each R matches the R&A dominant mode and develops the behavioural norms and dispositions the competency describes.

assessment_items.task: Using only old newspaper or used paper, make one paper toy or decoration of your choice — a fan, a twisted figure, or a paper bird. Attach a small label to your item that states: (1) what the item is, (2) what paper it was made from, and (3) which R of the 5Rs your item demonstrates.
assessment_items.scaffold: My item is a ___. It is made from ___. It demonstrates the R called ___ because ___.
format_of_output: A handmade paper toy or decoration from old/used paper
A written label with three pieces of information
assessment_items.annotation: Assess both the object and the label. The label must correctly name Repurpose (or Recycle with a valid reason) and give a reason that connects old paper to the principle. A fan made from a fresh sheet does not meet the brief.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Let Us Get Creative with Paper
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can transform a discarded everyday material into a new object and articulate the environmental principle that this action represents.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students demonstrate that they can physically enact the Repurpose principle and explain it in their own words, connecting creative making to environmental conservation.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The label's third line (which R and why) is the key evidence. Look for whether the student names Repurpose specifically and gives a reason that goes beyond 'because I used old paper' — ideally, the reason says something about saving trees or reducing waste.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: item is made from clearly identifiable old/used paper; label correctly identifies Repurpose and gives a connected reason. Weak: fresh paper used; label names the wrong R; reason is absent.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may work in pairs for the construction step. Students with fine-motor difficulties may tear and fold rather than cut. A simple folded fan counts fully.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The make-and-label format matches the C&E dominant mode and asks students to demonstrate, not just describe, the Repurpose principle.

assessment_items.task: Think about objects that can be made from paper pulp. Write the names of at least three such objects in your notebook. Then, for each of the five Rs, write one specific step you can take in your own life to reduce paper waste. Use the table format: R | My Action.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Objects from paper pulp: ___, ___, ___.

R | My Action
Refuse | ___
Reduce | ___
Reuse | ___
Repurpose | ___
Recycle | ___
format_of_output: List of at least three paper pulp objects
Table with one action per R
assessment_items.annotation: Award marks for (a) three plausible paper pulp objects and (b) five specific actions, one per R. Accept any objects that can realistically be made from paper pulp — papier-mâché bowls, seedling pots, paper clay toys, egg trays, and so on. Regional variation in examples is acceptable and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply a multi-principle conservation framework to their own daily context and generate specific, actionable commitments for each principle.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students show they can recall uses of paper pulp beyond standard paper sheets and apply each of the five conservation principles to their own life in a specific, actionable way.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that the three objects are genuinely pulp-based (not just paper items) and that the five actions are distinguishable from one another — a student who writes 'use less' for every R has not internalised the framework.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: objects are specific (seedling pots, papier-mâché bowl); actions name a concrete habit or item for each R. Weak: objects listed are just 'paper' items; actions are vague or repeated.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may ask elders or the teacher for ideas about paper pulp objects — the textbook prompt explicitly encourages this. Accept local or regional examples.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The list-and-table format mirrors the textbook's reflection structure and allows the teacher to see each R addressed separately.

assessment_items.question_text: Meera's family buys a lot of paper cups for guests. She wants to convince her family to change this habit. Using the 5Rs framework, write what Meera could say to her family. Explain which R applies, why it matters for the environment, and what the family could do instead.
look_for: Correctly identifies Refuse (or Reduce) as the relevant R and names it.
Explains why the habit harms the environment — paper cups mean more trees cut, more waste generated.
Proposes a realistic alternative — using reusable cups, glasses, or steel tumblers.
Acknowledges a possible constraint the family might face (cost, convenience) and addresses it.
Writing is structured as a persuasive argument, not just a list of facts.
assessment_items.annotation: This is an extended reasoning item. Look for whether the student applies the framework to a real household situation rather than merely reciting the 5Rs. A strong response shows awareness of both environmental impact and practical feasibility.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate conservation choices in the context of real constraints and construct a reasoned personal commitment to specific behaviour changes.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at two types of paper: tissue paper and cardboard. For each one, name one property and one use. Then explain: which of the two types of paper do you think uses more natural resources to produce? Give one reason.
expected_elements: Tissue paper: one property (thin, soft, absorbent) and one use (wiping, wrapping delicate items).
Cardboard: one property (thick, stiff, hard) and one use (boxes, packaging).
Cardboard uses more natural resources because it is thicker and requires more raw material (wood pulp) to produce.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per element. For the third element, accept any reasoning that connects thickness or quantity of material to resource use. Do not penalise if the student argues for tissue paper and provides a coherent reason.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can link the observed physical properties of a material to the natural resources required to produce it and propose a responsible use decision based on that connection.
